name: dotted-list?
summary: True when the object is a finite chain of pairs ending in something other than the empty list -- including a non-pair on its own.
explanation: SRFI-1 divides every object in the world into exactly three shapes, and dotted-list? recognises one of them. A proper list is a finite chain of pairs ending in '(). A circular list is a chain that loops. Everything else -- (1 . 2), (a b . c), and, importantly, any bare non-pair like 42 or a symbol -- is a dotted list, on the reading that a non-pair is a chain of zero pairs ending in a non-null value. That last clause surprises people and is the reason the partition is total: ask the three predicates about any object at all and exactly one says yes. Practically, dotted-list? is how you detect that a structure you were about to walk will not terminate at '(), and how association-list and tree code distinguishes a payload-carrying tail from a proper spine. It walks the chain, so it costs O(n), and on a circular argument it answers #f rather than hanging.

examples.note: (#t #f #f #t) -- the improper pair and the bare number are both dotted; the proper list and the empty list are not.

examples.code:
(define things (list '(a b) (cons 'k 'v) '() 'sym '(1 2 . 3)))
(display (list 'dotted (filter dotted-list? things)
               'proper (filter proper-list? things)))
(newline)
examples.note: (dotted ((k . v) sym (1 2 . 3)) proper ((a b) ())) -- every element lands in exactly one bucket.

examples.code:
(define (spine-and-tail x)
  (if (not (dotted-list? x))
      (list 'not-dotted x)
      (let loop ((p x) (n 0))
        (if (pair? p) (loop (cdr p) (+ n 1)) (list 'pairs n 'tail p)))))
(display (list (spine-and-tail '(1 2 . 9)) (spine-and-tail 'bare) (spine-and-tail '(1 2))))
(newline)
examples.note: ((pairs 2 tail 9) (pairs 0 tail bare) (not-dotted (1 2))) -- a bare atom really is a zero-pair dotted list, tail and all.

caveats: A non-pair, non-null object is dotted. (dotted-list? 42) is #t and (dotted-list? "s") is #t. This is correct SRFI-1 and it catches everyone once.
The empty list is NOT dotted -- it is the shortest proper list. Only '() has that status.
It walks the chain, so it is O(n) on the spine. Do not call it inside a loop over the same object.
On a circular list it answers #f, not an error and not a hang. The cycle detection is part of the contract.
It says nothing about the elements, only the spine. '((1 . 2) (3 . 4)) is a proper list of dotted pairs, so dotted-list? on it is #f.
usecases: Rejecting improper input at an API boundary before a walk that assumes it will reach '().
Distinguishing a rest-argument tail or association-list cell from a proper list in generic code.
Completing the three-way shape dispatch with proper-list? and circular-list?.

learn.concept: Every object is exactly one of proper, circular, or dotted -- and the surprising membership is that atoms are dotted.
learn.progression: Build (cons 1 2) and see it is dotted. Then build (cons 1 (cons 2 3)) and see the spine is two long. Then ask dotted-list? about the number 5, be surprised, and work out that a chain of zero pairs ending in 5 is exactly what 5 is. That is the moment the partition stops being three special cases and becomes one definition.

row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (spine-length x)
  (if (dotted-list? x)
      (let loop ((p x) (n 0)) (if (pair? p) (loop (cdr p) (+ n 1)) n))
      (or (length+ x) 'unbounded)))
(display (map spine-length (list '(1 . 2) '(1 2 3 . 4) 'atom '(1 2 3))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A queue accepts a payload from an untrusted caller and must reject anything it cannot safely walk. Candidates: dotted-list? (names the exact failure -- a finite spine with a junk tail -- and is safe on circular input, so it never hangs), list? (answers the question but collapses dotted and circular into one #f, so the rejection message cannot say which), a bare pair? test (accepts (1 . 2) happily, since that is a pair), walking with null? and catching the error (works, but discovers the problem by crashing and gives up the diagnosis), length (raises on improper input, which is a rejection but not a report). dotted-list? is the pick because the caller deserves to be told which of the two ways they were wrong.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: a three-way validator over a proper list, an improper one, and a bare symbol, which reports improper-tail rather than a crash. math: spine length, which for a dotted list counts pairs before the junk tail and for anything else falls back to length+, across four shapes including a zero-pair atom. cs: the partition displayed directly -- five objects, and each shows exactly one letter, which is the total-and-exclusive claim made visible.
row-2-audit.meta: The cs program is the whole reason the other two work. Because the three predicates partition rather than overlap, a cond over them is exhaustive and its else branch is reachable for exactly one shape.
row-2-audit.eng: A validator that says no is half a validator. Saying which no is what lets the caller fix the input rather than guess.
row-2-audit.math: Spine length is well defined for proper and dotted lists and undefined for circular ones. That is not a gap in the definition, it is the definition.
row-2-audit.cs: A total, mutually exclusive classification is what makes a dispatch safe to write as a cond with no fallthrough. Overlapping predicates make the order of clauses load-bearing.

row-3-dimension.setup: Deciding whether a chain of pairs stops at the empty list or at something else.

rungs.domain: a measurement chain where the final entry is a unit rather than another reading
rungs.code:
(define (reading-with-unit readings)
  (if (not (dotted-list? readings))
      (list 'no-unit readings)
      (let loop ((p readings) (vals '()))
        (if (pair? p)
            (loop (cdr p) (cons (car p) vals))
            (list 'values (reverse vals) 'unit p)))))
(display (list (reading-with-unit '(21 22 24 . celsius))
               (reading-with-unit '(101 . kilopascal))
               (reading-with-unit '(1 2 3))))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a macro expander deciding whether a lambda list has a rest parameter
rungs.code:
(define (arity formals)
  (cond ((proper-list? formals) (list 'fixed (length formals)))
        ((dotted-list? formals)
         (let loop ((p formals) (n 0))
           (if (pair? p) (loop (cdr p) (+ n 1)) (list 'at-least n 'rest p))))
        (else (list 'bad formals))))
(display (list (arity '(a b c)) (arity '(a b . rest)) (arity 'args) (arity '())))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare values it is a four-way sort and the answer is the whole output. On a measurement chain the dotted tail is CARRYING something -- the unit -- so the predicate is not rejecting the shape, it is licensing a walk that harvests both the readings and the tail, and the proper-list case is the one that has to report an absence. In a macro expander the same walk becomes arity computation: the number of pairs is the minimum argument count and the tail is the rest parameter's name, so one predicate plus one loop produces a complete calling convention, and the bare-symbol case -- a lambda list that is just (lambda args ...) -- is handled by the same branch because a symbol is a zero-pair dotted list. Same test; it goes from classifier, to extractor, to the thing that gives a language its calling convention.
row-3-dimension.meta: Rung three is why SRFI-1 counts atoms as dotted. A lambda list of 'args and a lambda list of '(a . args) want the same code path, and they get it only because a bare symbol is a dotted list of length zero.
row-3-dimension.eng: Putting a unit in the tail is a real encoding, not a curiosity -- it keeps the metadata attached to the data without wrapping every reading.
row-3-dimension.math: The spine length of a dotted list is a lower bound on arity. 'at least n' is precisely the statement that the tail absorbs the remainder.
row-3-dimension.cs: Every Lisp's lambda list is a dotted list, and the rest parameter is its tail. The shape of the parameter list IS the calling convention.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (exactly-one-shape? x)
  (= 1 (length (filter (lambda (b) b)
                       (list (dotted-list? x) (proper-list? x) (circular-list? x))))))
(display (map exactly-one-shape? (list '() '(1 2 3) (cons 1 2) 42 (circular-list 1 2) "s")))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (spine-pairs x)
  (let loop ((p x) (n 0)) (if (pair? p) (loop (cdr p) (+ n 1)) n)))
(define (length+-counts-the-spine? x)
  (cond ((dotted-list? x) (= (length+ x) (spine-pairs x)))
        ((proper-list? x) (and (= (length+ x) (length x)) (= (length+ x) (spine-pairs x))))
        (else (eq? (length+ x) #f))))
(display (map length+-counts-the-spine? (list (cons 1 2) '(1 2 . 3) 'a '() '(1 2 3) (circular-list 5))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (consing-makes-dotted? tail n)
  (let build ((k n) (acc tail))
    (if (= k 0)
        (eq? (dotted-list? acc) (not (or (null? tail) (proper-list? tail))))
        (build (- k 1) (cons k acc)))))
(display (map (lambda (p) (consing-makes-dotted? (car p) (cdr p)))
              (list (cons 'end 3) (cons '() 3) (cons 9 0) (cons '(a b) 2) (cons "t" 1))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: Exactly one of dotted-list?, proper-list?, and circular-list? holds for any object whatsoever; length+ counts the pairs in the spine for dotted and proper lists alike and answers #f only for circular ones; and consing any number of pairs onto a tail yields a dotted list precisely when the tail itself was neither null nor proper.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all objects x, exactly one of dotted-list?(x), proper-list?(x), circular-list?(x) is true; length+(x) = the number of pairs in x's spine when x is dotted or proper, and #f exactly when x is circular; and for all tails t and n >= 0, dotted-list?(cons^n(t)) = not(null?(t) or proper-list?(t))
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims: the partition is total and exclusive, length+ is the spine count wherever a spine terminates, and dottedness is inherited from the tail regardless of spine length. What would falsify them: an object matching two predicates or none, a dotted list whose length+ disagreed with a hand walk, or a spine whose classification changed as it grew. The bare symbol is in the second program because its spine has zero pairs, so length+ must answer 0 and not raise. The n=0 case in the third program tests the same atom clause from the other side -- consing nothing onto 9 must still be dotted.
row-4-proof.eng: The partition is what makes a three-branch cond safe. If two predicates could both hold, clause order would silently decide behavior.
row-4-proof.math: length is a partial function defined only on proper lists; length+ is its total extension, counting the spine wherever the spine ends and reporting #f where it does not. The single #f is the honest answer for the one shape with no finite count.
row-4-proof.cs: Dottedness is a property of the tail, propagated unchanged through any number of conses. That is why an improper structure never becomes proper by growing.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (improper? x) (dotted-list? x))
(define (split-spine x)
  (if (not (improper? x))
      (cons x '())
      (let loop ((p x) (front '()))
        (if (pair? p) (loop (cdr p) (cons (car p) front)) (cons (reverse front) p)))))
(define (normalize x)
  (let ((s (split-spine x)))
    (if (improper? x) (append (car s) (list (list 'tail (cdr s)))) (car s))))
(display (list 'dotted (normalize '(1 2 . 9))
               'proper (normalize '(1 2 3))
               'atom (normalize 'z)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (has-junk-tail? x) (dotted-list? x))
(define (tail-of x)
  (if (has-junk-tail? x)
      (let loop ((p x)) (if (pair? p) (loop (cdr p)) p))
      '()))
(define (tail-histogram xs)
  (let loop ((r xs) (atoms 0) (propers 0))
    (cond ((null? r) (list 'junk-tails atoms 'clean propers))
          ((has-junk-tail? (car r)) (loop (cdr r) (+ atoms 1) propers))
          (else (loop (cdr r) atoms (+ propers 1))))))
(display (list 'tails (map tail-of (list '(1 . 2) '(1 2) 'q))
               'census (tail-histogram (list '(1 . 2) '(1 2) 'q '() '(3 . 4)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (rest-arg? formals) (dotted-list? formals))
(define (calling-convention formals)
  (if (rest-arg? formals)
      (let loop ((p formals) (n 0) (names '()))
        (if (pair? p)
            (loop (cdr p) (+ n 1) (cons (car p) names))
            (list 'min n 'fixed (reverse names) 'rest p)))
      (list 'min (length formals) 'fixed formals 'rest #f)))
(define (accepts? formals argc)
  (let ((c (calling-convention formals)))
    (if (list-ref c 5) (>= argc (cadr c)) (= argc (cadr c)))))
(display (list (calling-convention '(a b . more))
               'checks (map (lambda (n) (accepts? '(a b . more) n)) '(1 2 5))
               'fixed (map (lambda (n) (accepts? '(a b) n)) '(1 2 5))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: dotted-list? answers whether a chain of pairs ends in junk instead of the empty list.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: improper? is one call; split-spine uses it to decide whether to walk at all, and normalize calls it AGAIN to decide how to render the result, so improper structure gets converted into proper structure with the tail preserved as data rather than discarded. math: has-junk-tail? is one call; tail-of extracts the terminator and tail-histogram counts how many members of a heterogeneous collection carry one, which is a data-quality audit built from a shape test. cs: rest-arg? is one call; calling-convention turns a lambda list into an arity contract, and accepts? then answers whether a given argument count is legal -- which is the entire front half of a procedure-call implementation.
row-5-emergence.meta: Every composition here calls its helper at least twice, in different roles: once to decide whether to walk, once to decide how to report. That doubling is the tell that the predicate is a real branch in the program's logic and not a validation afterthought.
row-5-emergence.eng: Normalising improper input into proper structure with the tail tagged is how you accept generous input without letting it infect everything downstream.
row-5-emergence.math: A census over shapes is the first thing to run on a corpus you did not create. The counts tell you which code paths will actually be exercised.
row-5-emergence.cs: Arity checking is a shape question about the lambda list, answered before any argument is evaluated. Getting it from dotted-list? is why Lisps never needed a separate arity syntax.
